extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students of literature and humor, writers and comedians interested in wit
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what constitutes 'wit' and its common forms (quip, repartee, witticism, wisecrack), useful for understanding or producing clever, typically short humorous remarks. Focuses on qualities like cleverness, spontaneity, wordplay, and rhetorical effect rather than strict laugh-centered comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: wit as intelligent humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit is a form of intelligent humour — the ability to say or write things that are clever and typically funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises cleverness and intelligence in expression; being 'typically funny' is part of wit but the cognitive cleverness is central. Use this as the baseline criterion for classifying remarks as 'wit'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witty person: spontaneous one-line or single-phrase jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone witty, also known as a wit, is a person skilled at wit, making spontaneous one-line or single-phrase jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights spontaneity and brevity as typical performance features of wit—skill at producing concise, often off-the-cuff lines is a marker of a witty speaker or writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of wit (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of wit include the quip, repartee, and wisecrack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as distinct subgenres or vehicles for wit; choosing the appropriate form shapes expectations about length, timing, and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quip
rubrics_metrics.description: A quip is an observation or saying that has some wit but perhaps descends into sarcasm, or otherwise is short of a point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quips are typically brief observational remarks; they may trade on sarcasm and sometimes lack a fully developed point—effective when brevity and a sharp edge are desired, but risk feeling flippant or unsubstantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witticism (diminutive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A witticism also suggests the diminutive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies a smaller-scale, lighter jest compared with a full-fledged epigram or elaborate piece of wit; useful when a light, polished turn of phrase is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repartee: quick comeback and retort
rubrics_metrics.description: Repartee is the wit of the quick answer and capping comment: the snappy comeback and neat retort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritises speed and conversational timing—repartee works best in dialogic settings where promptness and a neat reversal or cap make the remark effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit may be intentionally cruel or more ingenious than funny
rubrics_metrics.description: Witty remarks may be intentionally cruel (as also in many epigrams), and perhaps more ingenious than funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that wit can aim to sting or to display intellectual cleverness rather than to produce laughter; effective wit can therefore serve social or rhetorical functions (e.g., insult, critique, display of intellect) and may trade off warmth for ingenuity. Examples include Dorothy Parker/Algonquin Round Table style remarks and epigrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit in metaphysical poetry: wordplay combined with conceptual thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: It may combine word play with conceptual thinking, as a kind of verbal display requiring attention, without intending to be laugh-out-loud funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In verse (e.g., John Donne and metaphysical poetry) wit often manifests as intricate conceits and wordplay that reward attentive readers; humour can be subtle or secondary to intellectual display, so evaluate such wit on cleverness and conceptual integration rather than on outright comedic effect.
